Dodge Ram Truck Looks Beat Up Until You Pop the Hood
17 photos
Photo: Magnacars | YouTube
You wouldn't give a dime for this 1994 Dodge Ram 1500. It is a beat-up, run-down, moss-covered truck that was left to rot for a few years before it was rescued. However, a diesel mechanic paid $6,000 to take it home and says it might have been worth much more.
Luckily, the massive downpour in which TJ Lamb from Magnacars films alongside David, the new owner of the truck, might wash away years of neglect. David is a diesel mechanic who also builds turbos and one who can’t stand to see a car left to rot. He bought this 1994 Dodge Ram 1500 from someone who no longer needed it. But he did, and had big plans with it.
The Dodge Ram had been a burnout truck before it was abandoned, and it had already been V10-swapped. The donor engine came from a 1998 Viper GTS that was wrecked by the previous owner at just 30,000 to 40,000 miles (48,280 to 64,374 kilometers) on the clock. So he swapped it into the truck.
" Nobody would believe how much I bought it for, " David says, because he knows he got lucky. He paid $6,000 for the truck. The V10 alone would have been an $8,000 deal without even sitting under the hood of a vehicle. Everything about the engine was fine, but he couldn't say the same about the truck that it came with.
Photo: Magnacars | YouTube Abandoned for years, covered in dust and grime, with green moss growing on top of the white paint, partially enveloping the truck in green, it looked like the earth had started to claim it. That is just Pacific Northwest kind of patina. The weather is anything but kind in the area. David is keeping that original patina for the moment, but at some point, he is going to swap this look for an RT/10 concept truck from the 1990s.
Nope, Dodge never built that concept truck, but David will, with inspiration from the 1996 Dodge Ram VTS. “Similar but in my own style.” He will also install 18-inch Viper wheels with grippier tires, Mickey Thompsons on the rear axles, because he will need all the grip he can get when he hits the drag strip. He will also put on bigger brakes because he will need all the braking power he can get.
The new owner has had the truck since February and has been working on it since. There is always something he has to fix. His Dodge Ram is, after all, a 32-year-old truck. When he brought it home, it was an absolute mess. The front suspension was shot, the brakes were useless, the steering didn’t work, and the clutch was blown.
It came with the T56 six-speed manual transmission from the Viper, but it didn’t shift, so he installed a Tremec TR-6060 out of a 2008 fourth-generation Viper. Now, he is running a twin-disc clutch setup, capable of withstanding up to 1,000 horsepower. He is still far behind that. The V10 now makes between 600 and 700 horsepower at the wheel.
Photo: Magnacars | YouTube David dropped the truck on Belltech drop spindles up front to make it look more aggressive, as if it didn't already, with its grille-less front end and fans and radiator exposed. Everything is there for a reason, while the truck looks like the ultimate sleeper.
The rear still sits at its standard height, but David plans to drop it four inches. The truck is sitting on a 9-inch rear end, but it has a 3.50 Positraction in it, which is a little too tall for the six-speed, David complains. At 80 mph (129 kph) in the sixth gear on the highway, he is at only 1,200 rpm. So there is plenty of room for more. And he seems determined to get more.
Now, he is daily driving the 32-year-old truck just for the fun of it. He does burnouts in it and plans to drag race it with a new setup. He has taken it to car meets, and he must admit his truck was the shock factor of the event every time. The beat-up Ram makes tons of power, and the Valvetronic 3-inch mufflers roar out all the drama from under the hood.
David will also swap the factory seats for a pair of Viper buckets and a vintage instrument cluster. Right now, he's got wires dangling from the dashboard, but it's getting better. At least the dashboard is not cracked after so many years of neglect. But the windshield is.
Photo: Magnacars | YouTube
How many miles does the truck have on the clock right now? Well, the owner has no idea. The odometer stopped working at 166,000 miles (267,151 kilometers).
David also drives around in a lifted 2015 Volkswagen Golf TDI , looking like a rally car, while working on a 1991 Golf that he TDI-swapped. The next move is to make it all-wheel drive.
